en: May there be no obstacle!
While residing on the delightful peak of Kailāsa, Maheśvara spoke thus to Bṛhaspati regarding the unsurpassed reality of Śiva.

Lord Īśvara resided on Mount Kailāsa, where he remained in seclusion, venerating all the deities. At that time, a certain [being] bestowed upon him the *śāstra* of worship for the Supreme Cause, the Lord. At that time, there was a priest (*viku*) in heaven named Bhagavān Vṛhaspati. He came to offer worship to the Lord with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*). After he had finished offering worship, he prostrated himself. After he had finished prostrating, he sat down to receive the essence of all the sacred teachings. He spoke thus:
O Blessed One, God of gods, primordial Supreme Lord,
please explain the entirety of reality while delighting all that is moving and unmoving.

"O Lord, please grant us, O Lord Rāṇaka, instruction on all the noble and venerable ones (*saṅ hyaṅ aji kabeh*). There are many divisions among them, O Lord, which have been taught by You to all the *vatěk* deities. Some are called Śaiva, some are called Pāśupata, and some are called Alepaka. All of these are indeed various teachings granted by You repeatedly. Furthermore, there are many kinds of scriptures (*śāstra*) with many varieties. What is the reason for this? Why does the Lord grant so many paths along with His teachings? Thus spoke Bhagavān Vṛhaspati. The Lord replied, speaking as follows:
Excellent, excellent, O Mahāsattva! That which is the reality of the fruit of karma is indeed endowed with existence both in this world and in the next.

“O Venerable Bṛhaspati, what is the ultimate cause of this? It is because of the multitude of births that I have been granted this noble knowledge by all the gods. Since there are many wombs (yoni), there must be a reason for their creation. What is it that causes them to be so numerous? It is because the name ‘vāsanā’ is many. Vāsanā means the karma performed during one’s life here; its fruit is experienced in the world beyond, in subsequent births—whether they be miserable or auspicious. Whatever karma one performs, even if it is very small, its fruit does not perish. It is like the scent of asafoetida (hiṅgu) that has soaked into a cloth: once the asafoetida has vanished, the cloth still retains the scent; the fragrance remains inherent in the cloth. Such is the nature of vāsanā. It is exactly the same with what is called *karmavāsanā*. It exists within the self (*ātman*), and the *karmavāsanā* is indeed inherent in it. This causes the self to become agitated; when the self is agitated, that is what is called passion (*rāga*). Vāsanā stirs up this passion, which is the reason why one desires to perform karma. All the joy derived from *karmavāsanā* causes the vāsanā to further agitate the self, thereby stimulating both the *karmavāsanā* and the karma itself. This brings about birth in various forms: there is birth in the womb of a god, birth in the womb of a *vidyādhara*, birth in the womb of a *rākṣasa*, birth in the womb of a *daitya*, and birth in the womb of a *nāga*. There are many varieties of wombs through which one is born; that is why their appearances are diverse. Whatever the mind of one’s previous womb was accustomed to, that is what one desires. That desire then stimulates the karma, which one performs again and again. If the karma one performs is evil, it causes one to fall into hell, where one experiences the fruits of all the *saṃsāra*. Once the fruit of one’s evil deeds has perished, it grants one birth as an animal. But if the karma one performs is auspicious, it causes one to dwell in heaven, where one enjoys all manner of pleasures. Once the fruit of one’s good deeds has perished, it grants one birth as a wealthy king or a lord of great riches. One becomes possessed of excellent wisdom, perceives all things clearly, and attains both tranquility and devotion through merit. All these things come about through that connection to the grace of the Lord; the Lord still dwells within them. One sees the *janmavāsanā* within them, along with thirst, heat, suffering, and the afflictions of being created. As long as one is subject to these, one suffers the extreme pain of birth, and in the end, one only experiences the fire of suffering. What is the way to escape from this state of mine? It is by approaching a wise man (*paṇḍita*) who understands the nature of existence and is instructed by a seer (*ṛṣi*). However, if one lacks such [instruction], one will only receive a particular kind of birth. That is why one should diligently seek much noble knowledge. Whatever one possesses, one should offer in devotion to the Lord; that is what one should take up as one’s own wisdom to be grasped by the Lord. Such is the reason why noble knowledge is so manifold. Thus spoke the Lord. Bhagavān Bṛhaspati replied: “What then is the distinction of that divine wisdom? By the command of the Lord, the Śaiva, the Pāśupata, and the Ālepaka are all distinct. The Lord replied: “There is no inferior and no superior among the heavens, O my son, if one follows the path correctly. For I have already explained that the three paths are all equally auspicious. If one errs in understanding the wisdom, there is something else [different]; that is why it is called deluded wisdom (*bhrānta-jñāna*). It is difficult to overcome. Thus spoke the Lord. Bhagavān Bṛhaspati said: “What is this deluded wisdom of which the Lord speaks? Because the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*) are true, and the wise men who practice meritorious devotion follow them—that is why the Lord calls it deluded wisdom. Please, O Son of the Lord, grant us your grace and instruction. Thus spoke Bhagavān Bṛhaspati. The Lord replied: “Listen.”

Blind men, joined together by the blind, in order to grasp the body of an elephant, each, failing to perceive its true likeness through their own eyes, wander about in confusion because of one another. (4)

“There is something called *samoha* (delusion), which is like a blind person who does not know the nature of the face (*liman*). Because of his acceptance [of that state], he comes to know it; yet he is blind and must be guided by someone who knows the face. However, as he is led along step by step, there are those who lead him by the head, comparing the face to a water-jar; others lead him by the ears, comparing the face to a fish-hook; others lead him by the nose, comparing the face to a plowshare; others lead him by the forehead, comparing the face to a high ridge; others lead him by the cheek, comparing the face to a bamboo joint; others lead him by the leg, comparing the face to a pillar. Whatever part they lead him by, he errs in every place, for he does not know the likeness of the face. In its presentation, he only knows its physical form, its shape, and its color; he does not know why it is a face. He only knows what has been led before him. This is like the state of one whose essence is blindness: he does not know the likeness of the face. Such is birth; this is what is meant by *vyāmoha* (delusion). It serves as the foundation for the blind person’s delusion. The essence of the face consists of various parts: the head, the neck, the nose, the forehead, the legs, and so forth. Thus, the scriptures and the teachings have many applications regarding the specific characteristics of the Divine Being (*sāṅ hyaṅ viśeṣa*). That is the reason why one becomes confused and wanders astray, falling into error. One is confused about east and west; one is confused about value and distinction; one is confused about near and far; one is confused about small and large; one is confused about low and high. Knowledge such as this is what is called *bhrānta* (error). It does not clarify the purpose. Thus spoke the Lord. Bhagavān Vṛhaspati replied: “Thus spoke the Lord.”
O Blessed One, knower of all reality, beginningless Supreme Lord!
O Blessed One, I desire to hear from you this which contains all reality.

"O Lord, my lord, there is great doubt regarding this principle of darkness (*andhatattva*). Is there any resemblance between it and the knowledge of the principles (*tattvajñāna*) of the Holy One, which is used to penetrate all the scriptures? May my lord grant me his grace; let him explain it clearly so that the confusion in my lord’s mind may vanish. Thus spoke Bhagavān Vṛhaspati. The Lord replied: "What you have said, Bhagavān Vṛhaspati, is most excellent. It is indeed possible to comprehend that knowledge of the principles of the Holy One. However, your effort must be directed toward the Holy Scriptures (*śāstra*), for you are to be instructed by me. You are to be instructed in the Holy Teaching (*āgama*), for you have been made a teacher in the world and in heaven, while your disciples shall propagate it among humanity. Thus he spoke.
Reality is twofold: supreme consciousness and the unconscious.
It pervades all principles; it is subtle and must be inferred with effort. (6)

Now, the manner in which these principles (*tattva*) are differentiated: they are *cetana* (conscious) and *acetana* (unconscious). *Cetana* means that whose essential nature is knowledge (*jñānasvabhāva*), which knows and is not subject to forgetfulness; it is eternally enlightened (*nityomiḍeṅ*) at all times and is without obstruction. That is what is called *cetana*. *Acetana* means that which lacks knowledge, like a stone; that is what is called *acetana*. When this *cetana* and *acetana* meet, they produce all the principles (*sarvatattva*). Their forms are: the principle of primordial matter (*pradhānatattva*), the principle of the three qualities (*triguṇatattva*), the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), the principle of ego (*ahaṅkāratattva*), the principle of the external senses (*bāhyendriyatattva*), the principle of the organs of action (*karmendriyatattva*), and the principle of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūtatattva*). These are what are called "all the principles. You must understand them thoroughly. Now, listen to their characteristics as we explain them to you. There are three individual types of *cetana*. Their forms are: the principle of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśivatattva*), the principle of Sadāśiva (*sadāśivatattva*), and the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). These are the three types of *cetana* that follow one another. As for the principle of Supreme Śiva: [it is... [text continues].
Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from affliction;
subtle, omnipresent, eternal, constant, immutable, and sovereign.
(7) It is immeasurable because it is infinite, and indescribable because it is without defining characteristics.
It is incomparable and invisible because it is stainless, and it is free from affliction.
It is subtle because it is unperceivable, and it is all-pervading because of its omnipresence.
Its emptiness is eternal by nature, and it is steadfast because it is immovable.
Because it is completely full, it is imperishable, and likewise possesses a serene nature;
this is called the Śiva-principle, which is omnipresent and perfectly established.

O immeasurable Lord! That which is beyond the reach of the senses; what is the reason? Because of its state as the infinite (*ananta*); it is not contained within anything (*tan pahiṅan*); it is indefinable (*anirdeśyam*); it cannot be pointed out (*tan patuduhan*); because of its state as being without characteristics (*tan palakṣaṇa*); it is incomparable (*anaupamyam*); it cannot be illustrated (*tatan papaḍa*); because of its state as having no likeness even unto itself (*tan hana paḍa nira juga*); it is free from affliction (*anāmayam*); it is never subject to disease (*tatan keneṅ lara*); because of its state as being eternal (*alilaṅ*); it is subtle (*sūkṣma*), for its state is such that it cannot be perceived by the senses; it is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*) and omnipresent (*sarvagata*), for it has permeated all realms; it encompasses everything (*sahananya kabeh*); it is eternally manifest at all times (*nityomiḍeṅ sadākāla*), for its state is one of non-obstruction (*tan pasaṅkan*); it is constant (*dhruvam*), for its state is one of immobility; it is eternally manifest at all times (*umiḍeṅ sadākāla*); it is immutable (*avyayam*), for its state is one of perfection (*paripūrṇa*); it is the Sovereign (*īśvara*), for the term *īśvara* refers to its state as the supreme Lord (*prabhu*). It is the ultimate authority (*pramāṇa*) that is itself not subject to being measured or proven. This is what is called the *paramaśivatattva* (the Supreme Śiva Principle). This is what is called the *sadāśivatattva* (the Sadāśiva Principle), which lies below the *paramaśivatattva*.
Śiva, accompanied by activity, is Sūrya; Sadāśiva is the principle of consciousness (caitanya-tattva).
Endowed with stations and qualities, he is all-pervasive; yet because he is formless, he is not perceived.
He is the progenitor, not the accomplisher [of rituals], for he is solely intent upon bestowing grace.
He is the eternal maker of light, omniscient, the all-creating, omnipresent Lord.
He is considered the protector for the helpless; he is regarded as their brother, their mother, and their father.
In birth after birth, he is the deliverer from all suffering.

Possessing activity; Lord Sadāśiva is the head. He holds the lotus-seat and the *pinaka* bow. Furthermore, that which is called the lotus-seat is his *śakti*. As for *śakti*, it consists of the pervasive power (*vibhuśakti*), the sovereign power (*prabhuśakti*), the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). These are the fourfold powers. Now, as for what is called the pervasive power (*vibhuśakti*): "This world, both woven across and woven lengthwise, is by Śiva, the Supreme Lord. 'Woven across' means pervaded; 'woven lengthwise' is like a thread through jewels. (14)

The nature of *ūta* is that it pervades all principles (*sarvatattva*). Its nature is to be pervasive, like a thread woven through pearls; though the pearls are visible, the thread itself is not seen—this is what is called *ūta*. *Prota* is like a string of jewels: just as the jewels occupy different positions along the string, so too does the *ūta-prota* (the warp and woof) exist. This is called *vibhu-śakti* (the pervasive power), for it causes all things to exist. *Prabhu-śakti* (the sovereign power) is that which is unobstructed throughout all realms. This is the *cadu-śakti* (fourfold power) in the form of a lotus. In its center is the place where the Lord (*Bhaṭāra*) resides at the time of His manifesting a body. He is the *mantrātmā*; the *mantra* is His body. *Īśāna* is His head; *Tatpuruṣa* is His face; *Aghora* is His heart; *Vāmadeva* is His private parts; *Sadyojāta* is His form. *Oṃ*. Such is the body of the Lord, radiant with the color of crystal. These are the qualities (*guṇa*) in Him: He hears from afar, He knows all from afar, and He sees from afar. "Hearing from afar" means perceiving sounds from a distance without effort. "Knowing all from afar" means knowing the secrets of those far away. "Seeing from afar" means seeing everything far away; these are the qualities. He possesses the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*): *aṇimā* (minuteness), *laghimā* (lightness), *mahimā* (greatness), *prāpti* (attainment), *prākāmya* (efficacy), *īśitva* (lordship), *vaśitva* (control), and *yatrakāmāvasāyitva* (the power to resolve according to one's will). These constitute the inherent nature of the Lord. This is the *sadāśiva-tattva*. Below this *sadāśiva-tattva* is the *māyāśiras-tattva*. Here reside the eight deities of the *vidyāsana*: Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivatama, Ekarudra, Ekanetra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍī. Lord Ananta is appointed by the Lord to govern the worlds and the universe. Yet he is also subject to further activity of the self (*ātma-vyāpāra*) once commanded by the Lord. When Lord Ananta has completed his task, Lord Sūkṣma takes over from Ananta; Śivatama from Sūkṣma; Ekarudra from Śivatama; Ekanetra from Ekarudra; Trimūrti from Ekanetra; and Śrīkaṇṭha from Trimūrti. As for Śikhaṇḍī, he says: "I am Śrīkaṇṭha. I was made to bestow knowledge upon the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). I was bound by the passion of the Lord Kāma. I was tormented by the divine Kāma; the reason I was tormented was because of his poisonous gaze. Suddenly, the divine Kāmadeva was reduced to ashes, turned to cinders. But my passion remained within me; that is why I became the husband of the Goddess Umā, who gave birth to Sanatkumāra. Such is the nature of Lord Anaku, the son of Bṛhaspati. The Rudras below him are consumed by me and brought upward. He who succeeds Śikhaṇḍī is he. This is the *māyāśiras-tattva*. Below the *māyāśiras-tattva* is the *māyā-tattva*. The *māyā-tattva* is empty and insentient (*acetana*), existing alongside the *śiva-tattva*, yet its inherent nature is insentience. Thus, it is subordinate to the *śiva-tattva*. It is pervaded by the *śiva-tattva*; its inherent nature is sentience (*cetana*), yet it is woven as the warp and woof by the *śiva-tattva*. The *ūta* (warp) is pervasive and omnipresent throughout the substance of *māyā*, while the *prota* (woof) occupies specific places. The *śiva-tattva* is inherently the warp within *māyā*; this is why it is stained by impurity (*mala*). Impurity is the state of being insentient, for the *śiva-tattva* is like a crystal-colored stone, stainless, pure, and radiant, having sentience as its inherent nature. It is stained by the insentient; thus its power (*śakti*) is lost. Power is the capacity to know all and to do all. Now the *śiva-tattva* is omniscient and the performer of all actions; this is what is called the *ātman*. Sentience is its very essence. There are many such *ātma-tattvas*, which is why they are equal to the *māyā-tattva*. It is like the house of a weaver, with layers upon layers. *Māyā* is the house of the weaver; the *ātman* is the weaver’s child. It is said to be "downward-facing," meaning the *ātman* is rooted below and does not know the principles above it. The *māyā-tattva* is then activated by the power of the Lord, and the *pradhāna-tattva* emerges. The *māyā* is manifold, empty, and insentient. The *ātma-tattva* and the *pradhāna-tattva* are both activated by the Lord. The *ātman* becomes insentient and forgetful, for it lacks primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). The *pradhāna-tattva* pervades it, causing the *ātman* to lose consciousness; this is the *pradhāna-tattva*. The *pradhāna-tattva* is then activated by the Lord’s power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) to produce the *triguṇa-tattva*. The *triguṇa-tattva* consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Sattva is light and illuminating; rajas is mobile and active; tamas is heavy and obscuring—this is the definition of the mind (citta). That which is great and expansive is called *sattva*; that which is agitated and turbulent is called *rajas*; that which is dull and dark is called *tamas*.

Liberation, heaven, hell, the state of an animal, and human birth arise from the evil of the mind, indeed through the power of the mind. (16) The mind is the cause of the self’s liberation and heaven; the mind is the cause of the self’s descent into hell; the mind is the cause for being born as an animal; the mind is the cause for the birth of a human; and the mind is the cause for attaining both liberation and bliss. This is the underlying principle here.

Uprightness, non-attachment, gentleness, generosity, lordliness, skillfulness, sweetness, and elegance of appearance—these are the characteristics of the *sāttvika* mind. Now, as for the *rajas* (the quality of passion): it is that which is firm and persistent; it knows the true nature of objects and their boundaries; it knows the principle of lordship (*īśvaratattva*); it is clever; it speaks with sweetness and charm; and its physical form is well-proportioned. Cruelty, arrogance, recklessness, ferocity, greed, fickleness, mercilessness, and negligence—these are the characteristics of the mind known as *rajas*. As for cruelty, it is the state of being wrathful, prone to anger, and impulsive; arrogance is being haughty and reckless; ferocity is greediness, having restless hands and feet, and being quick-tongued; mercilessness is lacking affection and being prone to biting with the teeth. These are the characteristics of the mind characterized by *rajas*. Now, as for *tamas*: * Heaviness, sleepiness, sloth, laziness, delusion, fear, sorrow, intoxication, and procrastination—these are the characteristics of the mind known as *tamas*. As for heaviness, it is the state of being dull, sluggish, and slow to act; sleepiness is the state of being drowsy and prone to dozing off; sloth is the state of being indolent and lacking vigor; laziness is the state of being idle and disinclined to work; delusion is the state of being confused and lacking discernment; fear is the state of being terrified and anxious; sorrow is the state of being distressed and grieving; intoxication is the state of being intoxicated and lacking self-control; procrastination is the state of being dilatory and failing to act promptly. These are the characteristics of the mind characterized by *tamas*. Now, as for *sattva*: * Lightness, clarity, joy, contentment, faith, fortitude, compassion, lack of greed, lack of delusion, and lack of fear—these are the characteristics of the mind known as *sattva*. The mind that is utterly pure (*sāttvika*), untainted, and like the inner space, has attained the state of being composed of ether; this is what is promised as universal liberation.

That which is the pure mind is the cause for one to grasp the Self for the sake of liberation, because it is stainless and easily able to comprehend the essence of the scriptures and the instructions of the Guru.

The state of equilibrium (*samatva*) of *rajas* is declared to be *dharma*; therefore, one desires auspiciousness through it. Why is *sattva* conjoined with that very same path leading to heaven? Because when *sattva* is not devoid of *rajas*, it is considered that the Lord’s *dharma* is desired by it; whenever its *dharma* is practiced, it returns to heaven, for *sattva* desires virtuous action while *rajas* causes it to fall.
The mind, deluded by the three qualities, is well-sounding yet deceptive; its state of self-conceit and impurity is desired as the fruit of human existence. 22

Furthermore, there are three qualities (*guṇa*): *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. These are the causes of birth as a human being, for they provide the impetus for one’s actions. *Rajas* is described as wicked and it seizes hold of *sattva*; *tamas* is described as base and dull, and it obscures *rajas*. *Sattva* and *rajas* together are described as good, yet they are constrained by *tamas*. Such is the mutual conflict of these three qualities; that is why no action can be performed by the *ātman* regarding what is good or evil. If an action—whether good or evil—were performed by the *ātman*, then it would be impossible for a human being to be born; this would be something desired by Lord Vidhi (the Creator) in the interval between heaven and hell, which would mean the *ātman* has attained liberation (*paśucyan*). Whoever performs any action at all to become a human being, this is what is intended by Lord Vidhi, for he [Vidhi] is the witness of the Lord regarding the auspicious and inauspicious karma of a living being’s birth.
The mind that is excessively *rājasa* is solely attached to anger and the like;

it is indeed the progenitor of fire—who, then, would be one whose seven limbs consist of fire? (23) When the mind is filled with *rajas*, it is exclusively [bound] by anger; it is as if it were given over to fire. That is the cause for the self to go to hell, and it causes all of *saṃsāra* to burn.
The mind that is excessively tamasic is intent on sleep and utterly deluded;
it is stationary, yet quickly returning [to its state], for that is certain from the activity of the mind.

When the mind (*citta*) dwells in darkness (*tamas*), that is the cause for the self (*ātman*) to produce the animal realm (*tiryak*). There are five types of animals; their forms are: domestic animals (*paśu*), wild beasts (*mṛga*), birds (*pakṣin*), reptiles (*sarīsṛpa*), and fish (*mīna*); finally, there are the immobile beings (*sthāvara*). *Paśu* refers to those that live in villages: cattle, buffaloes, dogs, and various kinds of livestock. *Mṛga* refers to creatures dwelling in the forest: lions, deer, elephants, and various kinds of forest animals. *Pakṣin* refers to all kinds of winged creatures: chickens, ducks, and various kinds of birds. *Sarīsṛpa* refers to all kinds of crawling creatures: scorpions, lice, fleas, and various kinds of worms. *Mīna* refers to all kinds of aquatic creatures: those in rivers, ponds, and the ocean, and so forth; all such things that move about in various ways are called mobile (*jaṅgama*). Such is the production of the self when it dwells in the quality of darkness. Because of this, one is unable to perform the means of attaining *dharma*. Why is it that one becomes mobile? That is the reason why, after five births, one produces [the state of] trees, shrubs, and various kinds of plants that do not move, which remain fixed in their very place—that is what is called immobile (*sthāvara*). Those that move are called mobile (*jaṅgama*). Such is the production of the self when it dwells in the mind characterized by darkness. From the three qualities (*triguṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*) arises. There are many types of intellect; its forms are as follows: virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). However, there are also their opposites: non-virtue (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). These are the five misconceptions (*pañcaviparyaya*). There is also contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and the eight perfections (*aṣṭasiddhi*). These are the functions (*vṛtti*) of the intellect. As for virtue (*dharma*): [it is defined as... (text continues).

Virtue, sacrifice, austerity, charity, renunciation, and indeed mendicancy, as well as yoga—in brief, these are the sole determination of Dharma. (25) Virtue (*śīla*) means guarding one’s conduct; sacrifice (*yajña*) means performing oblations with fire; austerity (*tapas*) means subduing the senses and their objects; charity (*dāna*) means giving; renunciation (*pravrajyā*) means the state of an ascetic who does not eat; mendicancy (*bhikṣā*) means the state of one who has been initiated; yoga means seeking meditative absorption (*samādhi*). These are the individual definitions of Dharma. Now, as for that which is called knowledge (*jñāna*):
Perception, inference, and the traditional teaching derived from the established doctrine—these three are declared to be the means of valid cognition; that is the supreme right knowledge. (26)

That which is supported by the three means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa)—namely, perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and scripture (āgama)—is as follows: perception means that which is seen directly; inference means, for example, when one perceives steam rising from afar and thereby infers the presence of fire; this is what is meant by inference. Scripture means the sacred teachings that are validated by the Guru; this is what is meant by scripture. That which is supported by these three means of valid knowledge—perception, inference, and scripture—is called right knowledge (samyagjñāna). Now, as for detachment (vairāgya):

Detachment from visible and heard enjoyments, as well as from happiness and the body—that is declared to be *vairāgya* (dispassion). A yogin is not one who is merely indifferent toward enjoyments. There are enjoyments that are seen, such as those of kings; there are enjoyments that are heard of, such as those of the gods in heaven. Regarding all these enjoyments, whether seen or heard of, he has no longing for them at all, because even the king himself has no longing for them. Therefore, this is called *vairāgya*. Now, as for what is called *aiśvarya* (sovereignty):
Furthermore, regarding enjoyments, secondary enjoyments, or consumable objects, that sovereignty should be understood by the wise as common to all three. 28

*Bhoga* means all that is eaten and drunk; *upabhoga* means all that is used for enjoyment; *paribhoga* means those things which we ourselves possess and are endowed with by them—that is what is called *aiśvarya*. These, namely *dharma*, *jñāna*, *vairāgya*, and *aiśvarya*, are the causes of the Lord’s grace toward the self (*ātman*). Now, their opposites are: *adharma*, *ajñāna*, *avairāgya*, and *anaiśvarya*. *Adharma* means the intellect (*buddhi*) that is deprived of *dharma*. Its discourse is as follows: "Who knows what is called heaven? What is its cause? What is the cause of hell? Sin comes from doing evil; how can one go to heaven by doing good? The words of the *maliṅ* (sorcerers) are false; a person who desires merit has a priest (*viku*) recite it for him. As for the *Veda*, it is merely a collection of words—the reason people follow a priest is because the words of the scripture are not manifest, for they are not seen to be governed [by reason]. Such is the discourse of the intellect devoid of *dharma*. *Ajñāna* means the intellect that is deprived of inference (*anumāna*), scripture (*āgama*), and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). When it is possessed by these, it becomes the cause for being possessed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and error (*bhrānta*). Conceptualization (*vikalpa*) means that which repeatedly imagines an object when it has been examined. Doubt (*saṃśaya*) means that which is characterized by uncertainty. Error (*bhrānta*) means that which is characterized by a mistaken understanding. That which is characterized by conceptualization, doubt, and error is what is called *ajñāna*. *Avairāgya* means the intellect that is intensely attached to objects—whether inferior, middling, or superior. Its discourse is: "What is the price now? This is more valuable. That is what is called *avairāgya*. *Anaiśvarya* means the intellect that is deprived of *bhoga*, *upabhoga*, and *paribhoga*; that is designated as *anaiśvarya*. Such are the opposites of the fourfold *aiśvarya*. What is the reason that the intellect endowed with *dharma* is said to be favored by the Lord? Herein lies the result:
Through dharma, one goes to heaven and is born among the divine races;

endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, one finds satisfaction in all enjoyments. Whatever dharma one performs with the intellect, that is the cause for returning to heaven; indeed, liberation in heaven consists of becoming a deity. One attains those qualities beginning with *aṇimā*. This, then, is the fruit of knowledge.

For by means of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), he who possesses the four powers is a wise man; having attained the state of liberation, he does not enter existence again. What is meant by "by means of right knowledge"? It is that he is most excellent, because he has attained liberation and does not undergo rebirth. What is meant by "possessing the four powers"? It is being called one who has reached the end of birth—that is, returning to the state of Śiva, his consciousness becoming of the same nature as the Lord. Now, here is the fruit of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Through dispassion (*vairāgya*), one dissolved into *prakṛti* attains happiness like one in deep sleep;

or, after a long period of time, one is born again among the divine classes (*devayoni*). This is what is meant by "dispassion": one merges into the world of *prakṛti*, remaining there for a very long time without waking up; thus he attains the happiness of that state, and finally becomes a deity. Such is the fruit of dispassion. Now, as for the fruit of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*):
Unimpeded in sovereignty, he is satisfied by all enjoyments;
endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, he is born among the divine classes of beings. || 32 ||

Thus, whatever his state may be and whatever his conduct, he experiences happiness in all its forms; finally, he becomes a deity and attains the qualities such as *aṇimā*. This is the fruit of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Now, the fruit of its opposite: when the intellect (*buddhi*) has unrighteousness (*adharma*) as its seed, it becomes an animal, for it suppresses righteousness. The fruit of knowledge (*jñāna*) is that which is the root of the happiness of action (*karmasukha*), because it leads upward toward the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). When good and evil deeds have been exhausted, that is the cause for being reborn as a human; hell and the animal realm are added to that. Indeed, the birth of a person who performs good deeds is rare; the reason many become animals is the consequence of committing evil. Lack of detachment (*avairāgya*) and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*) are what the Lord has forbidden. The self (*ātman*) has unrighteousness, ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of detachment, and lack of sovereignty as its seeds. Now, the five types of error (*pañcaviparyaya*): their forms are *tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*. *Tamas* is the intellect (*buddhi*) desiring to attain all forms of happiness. *Moha* is desiring to attain the eightfold sovereignty (*aṣṭaiśvarya*). *Mahāmoha* is desiring to attain happiness in the formless state (*niṣkala*) and the eightfold sovereignty. *Tāmisra* is when both happiness and the sovereignty one has attained are lost. *Andhatāmisra* is when a person grieves over things that have already vanished. These are the five errors; they are all the causes of the self’s wandering in *saṃsāra*. Now, the nine types of contentment (*tuṣṭi*): their forms are *arjana*, *rakṣaṇa*, *kṣaya*, *saṅga*, *hiṃsā*, *bhāgya*, *kāla*, and *ātmā*. *Arjana* is the acquisition of all wealth; guarding it is called contentment. *Rakṣaṇa* is the guarding of wealth already acquired; the anxiety of guarding wealth is itself contentment. *Kṣaya* is when a person reflects on suffering; even though the suffering is not yet great, the realization of its nature is contentment. *Saṅga* is meeting with loved ones; that is contentment. *Hiṃsā* is the act of killing or causing harm; that is external contentment (*bāhyatuṣṭi*). Now, the internal contentment (*ādhyātmikatuṣṭi*): *Bhāgya* is when the intellect is satisfied with its own nature and does not seek happiness. It says: "In the past there was no such thing as 'I'; my former actions were not good, which is why I do not meet with happiness now. Therefore, let this body of mine strive to perform good deeds, so that in future births I shall not suffer like this. That is contentment. *Kāla* is saying: "It is time for me to attain what I desire; what else can be said? For if it were not time, how could we have reached this point? That is contentment. *Ātmā* is the existence of knowledge capable of discerning the self through the grace of the Guru. That is the object of his knowledge; it does not exist by itself. One does not master that knowledge merely by receiving the teaching, because one has not practiced *samādhi*. Only when one is settled and satisfied within oneself is it contentment. These are the modes of contentment, which are the causes for the concealment of knowledge in those whose minds are satisfied. Now, the eight perfections (*aṣṭasiddhi*).
Generosity, study, grammar, logic, and friendship, as well as the three ways of destroying suffering—these are proclaimed as the eight accomplishments (siddhis). || 33 ||

*Dāna* (giving) is that which is the giving of one who possesses wealth; *adhyayana* (study) is that which is the learning of one who possesses wealth. There is also the practitioner (*sādhaka*), because of his intense practice of *sādhana*. He perceives subtle sounds; or else, there is one who possesses the capacity to examine all things, both gross and subtle. *Tarka* means the knowledge used for investigation; it is not erroneous in its investigation. This is called external perfection (*bāhyasiddhi*). Now, as for internal perfection (*ādhyātmikasiddhi*): it belongs to one who is able to dispel the three kinds of suffering. What are these three sufferings? They are: internal suffering (*ādhyātmika-duḥkha*), divine suffering (*ādhidaivika-duḥkha*), and elemental suffering (*ādhibhautika-duḥkha*). Internal suffering is that which arises from the mind. Its varieties are: passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*); fever, heaviness, hunger, thirst, vomiting, diarrhea, wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*śleṣma*), colic, and heartache. These are called internal suffering. Divine suffering is that which is caused by madness, insanity, possession, seizure by spirits (*graha*), and various other types of suffering arising from the gods. This is called divine suffering. Elemental suffering is being bitten, poisoned, struck by lightning, afflicted by poison, tormented, subjected to black magic (*abhicāra*), struck by a weapon, or targeted by wicked people and sorcerers. Various types of pain and suffering arising from living beings (*bhūta*)—where "living beings" refers to all animate creatures—this is called elemental suffering. He who is able to dispel such a multitude of sufferings is called one who has attained internal perfection. However, the person called one who has attained supreme perfection (*uttamasiddhi*) is the Lord of Yoga (*yogīśvara*), who has acquired the qualities beginning with *aṇimā*. Such is the function of the intellect (*buddhi*) which you have understood. From the intellect arises the ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), which is of three kinds. Its varieties are: *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. Such are its divisions. That which is *vaikṛta* is *sāttvika*; that which is *taijasa* is *rajas*; that which is *bhūtādi* is *tamas*. From the *vaikṛta* ego-consciousness arise the mind (*manas*) and the ten sense organs (*indriya*). Their varieties are: hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. From the *bhūtādi* ego-consciousness arise the five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*). It is the *taijasa* ego-consciousness that acts as the catalyst to bring about the manifestation of the products of the *vaikṛta* and *bhūtādi* ego-consciousness, for it has the nature of stimulating activity. What are called the five subtle elements? Listen, for I shall explain them to you. They are: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Their manifestations are as follows: when the ears are covered, sound exists; when one hears a sound, the essence of that sound perceived is called the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*). When there is a breeze blowing, the essence perceived by the skin through touch is called the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*). At twilight, when the sun has set, there is a light that appears; the essence of that light seen is called the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*). The subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) is that which is eaten, whether bitter or sweet; the essence of that taste perceived by the tongue which does not vanish when the person is no longer there, but remains as a residue, is called the subtle element of taste. The subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) is when there is sandalwood being rubbed; the essence of its fragrance smelled is called the subtle element of smell. Such are the five subtle elements. From the five subtle elements arise the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*). Space (*ākāśa*) arises from the subtle element of sound; air (*vāyu*) arises from the subtle element of touch; fire (*teja*) arises from the subtle element of form; water (*āpah*) arises from the subtle element of taste; earth (*pṛthivī*) arises from the subtle element of smell. These are the five great elements, which are all directly perceptible and manifest. Indeed, they are the limit of the principles (*tattva*) below. Such is the nature of all the principles. Each principle below serves as the support for the principles above it. Those principles below cannot be the supports for the principles above them. The principle of earth is the foundation of all the principles. Sound is the quality (*guṇa*) of space; touch is the quality of air; form is the quality of fire; taste is the quality of water; smell is the quality of earth. Furthermore, taste has six varieties. Their forms are: salty (*lavaṇa*), sour (*amla*), pungent (*kaṭuka*), bitter (*tikta*), astringent (*kaṣāya*), and sweet (*madhura*). Salty means briny; sour means acidic; pungent means hot; astringent means drying; sweet means sweet; bitter means acrid. These are the six tastes. The quality of earth is smell, which has two varieties: pleasant and unpleasant. Those six tastes are what are eaten and drunk by men and women; they produce life and the body. The essence of the body produces desire in men. Semen (*śukla*) is another [product]; menstrual blood (*śvanita*) is in the woman. When semen and blood meet at the center of the lotus-channel (*padmanāḍī*) within the six sheaths (*ṣaṭkoṣa*), that is what sustains life. In every way, through the union of semen and blood, whether as a human or as an animal, the form of whatever is born is produced according to the proportions of the semen relative to the blood. If the semen is more than the blood, it is male. If [the blood is more], it is female. If [they are equal], it is neuter. Thus ends the explanation.

The products [of the semen] are as follows: when the semen (*śukla*) is abundant, it produces the marrow (*vadvan*); however, when the quantity of the semen is small, it produces the marrow, bone, and brain. The blood (*śvanita*) becomes the flesh, blood, and skin; these three come from the male, and the other three from the female. This is what is called the "six sheaths" (*ṣaṭkoṣa*). The subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) becomes the ear, serving as the organ for perceiving sound. The subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*) becomes the skin, serving as the organ for perceiving touch. The subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*) becomes the eye, serving as the organ for seeing. The subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*) becomes the tongue, serving as the organ for tasting the six flavors (*ṣaḍrasa*). The subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) becomes the nose, serving as the organ for smelling various fragrances. These are the five organs of perception (*pañcabuddhīndriya*), for they are the physical seats (*golaka*) of the aforementioned senses. The organ of hearing (*śrotrendriya*) resides in the ear; it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the self (*ātman*) for perceiving sound. The organ of touch (*tvagindriya*) resides in the skin; it is the instrument of the self for perceiving touch. The organ of sight (*cakṣurindriya*) resides in the eye; it is the instrument of the self for seeing forms and colors. The organ of taste (*jihvendriya*) resides in the tongue; it is the instrument of the self for tasting the six flavors. The organ of smell (*ghrāṇendriya*) resides in the nose; it is the instrument of the self for smelling various fragrances. The organ of speech (*vāgindriya*) resides in the mouth; it is the instrument of the self for producing sound. The organ of the hand (*pāṇīndriya*) resides in the hands; it is the instrument of the self for grasping. The organ of the foot (*pādendriya*) resides in the feet; it is the instrument of the self for walking. The organ of excretion (*pāyvindriya*) resides in the anus; it is the instrument of the self for evacuating waste. The organ of generation (*upasthendriya*) resides in the male and female genitals; it is the instrument of the self for pleasure and for emitting semen and blood. Such is the sequence of the ten organs within the body. Bhagavān Vṛhaspati spoke: "Lord, please explain how the organs are activated by the Lord to perceive objects, and how they reside and function. The Lord spoke: "Vṛhaspati, you may ask this question. How can the physical seat (*golaka*) of the self be considered a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? Consider the ear: if the organ of hearing (*śrotrendriya*) is absent, one cannot hear sound even if the ear is intact. It is evident that even if the ear and its opening exist, one still cannot hear sound if the organ of hearing is not present. The same applies to the eye, which is the seat of sight: if it is completely white (blind), it is useless for seeing. Likewise, a blind person cannot perceive objects despite having eyes. Similarly, a person who is deaf or mute cannot perceive their respective objects if the organs are missing. You have seen all this, Vṛhaspati; therefore, the organs and their seats must be distinguished. The mind (*manas*) is the king of the organs; it conceives of objects because the organs are its subjects. 'To conceive' (*saṅkalpa*) means to direct the objects toward the organs so they may grasp them; this is the function of the mind. All the organs are not independent of their objects; indeed, it is pleasant to eat and drink, pleasant to walk about, pleasant to hear sweet sounds, and pleasant to enjoy various pleasures. This causes the divine self (*ātman*) to take birth in a body, for it is the self that brings all these things into being."
Pradhāna is like a cart, and Puruṣa is like a bull;
joined by Īśvara as the charioteer, the world revolves like a wheel. 34.

This body is the wheel of the cycle of rebirth; the good and evil karma is what is called the world. That which is cast into heaven or hell is the rim of the wheel of the cycle. The noble *ātman* is the hub that moves within the chariot; Lord *Īśvara* is the charioteer. As for this hub moving within the chariot, it is not that it does not move; rather, it is the cause of its being perceived. That is the seat of the *ātman*. It is the source from which the manifold enjoyments of the senses arise, following the abundance of the enjoyments it has consumed. That is the cause of the growth of passion (*rāga*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*drēmbha*), greed (*lobha*), envy (*mātsarya*), shamelessness (*prihati*), gluttony (*lapa*), arrogance (*vēlēkaṅ*), and the burden of suffering (*panasbhāran*). Such is the nature of all births. When the *ātman* is thus [bound], that is what is meant by the "reversed *ātman*" (*ātmā viparīta*). It is the object of its own subordination; it is made the hub by its own hub. Alas, such is its state! Thus comes the *ātman*. Its form is characterized by passion (*rāga-rāga*), because passion does not cease within human birth. Eating and sleeping are its specific characteristics. Alas, these eating and sleeping possess particular distinctions. Consciousness (*cetanā*) is diminished and obscured by darkness (*tamaḥ*), because the nature of eating is to consume and sleep. That sleep causes the *ātman* to forget; it forgets what it has practiced. Its essence is swallowed by the darkness of sleep. That is the reason it becomes cattle—oxen, buffaloes, dogs, pigs, ants, and various other kinds. Indeed, darkness is the cause of becoming cattle. That is the reason for producing trees, shrubs, roots, tubers, and various other plants. Such is the production of the *ātman*, arising manifoldly through the speech of passion. The Blessed Vṛhaspati spoke: "The *ātman* is exceedingly pure. This is the command of the Lord. How then can it fall into sin? That is the reason it is released from the sin of hell. Thus spoke the Blessed Vṛhaspati. The Lord spoke: "When the *ātman* returns to its true nature, when it is no longer obscured, the noble *ātman* alone experiences the pleasure and pain of the body, because it protects the integrity of the body. It seeks out all principles (*tattva*) in the substance of consciousness. It dissolves all the principles of the body; it is that which attains liberation. Its realization is as follows:"
The primary element is called the palace; the threefold end is proclaimed as the mantra.
They say the Śūdra is the sense organ, and the objects of experience are the pleasure of enjoyment. (35)

The body is the seat of authority; the three internal organs—namely the intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*)—are the seat of command. The senses are the seat of the subordinate officers and their attendants. The objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest—namely sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are the enjoyments to be eaten and drunk at all times. The divine Self (*ātman*) is the one who enjoys them, yet it seeks liberation from them all. The divine Self wanders through various states of enjoyment within this body; that is why it does not know its own nature, nor does it understand its own birth. The cause of this is as follows: because of the constant flickering of thoughts, it does not recognize the Self, and thus it receives the pleasures of the body. That is why it wanders through various existences, through various births, becoming a cow, a monkey, a human, and so forth—whatever kind of thing can provide pleasure—and it pursues these with great intensity. When that pleasure is encountered, it becomes the cause of suffering. The exhaustion of those who are weary, the crawling, the rolling about, the struggling, and the crying—all these are the exhaustion resulting from the pursuit of pleasure by the ten senses. Their functioning is like the spokes of a single hub; there are ten of them attached to that single hub. Because they do not function in unison, each acting separately, that single hub is the cause of *saṃsāra*. Vṛhaspati spoke, saying: "This is indeed the renunciation (*sanyāsan*) shown to Your Majesty. The characteristic of the Self existing within the body is that the mind (*citta*) and the Self are distinct; let this be explained to Your Majesty. The Lord spoke, saying: "Listen to its characteristics as you observe them. It is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) of the Lord that enters into the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). The ego enters into the vital air (*vāyu*), and that vital air is what connects the Self with the body. This is the sequence of its occurrence."

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the channels (*nāḍī*); listen to those which exceed three. They emerge from the one called *ahaṅkāra* at the navel, below the navel, in the bulbous root (*kanda*). [Commentary: As for what is meant by "channels" in the body: they arise from the center of the navel, their openings facing downward; they extend upward from the navel. This is the place where the vital breath (*ātata*) moves upward. It is the source of the various channels. There are three types of them.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā likewise arise;
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśas as well;
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
Now, O hero, I shall likewise declare the traditional teachings concerning the channels (nāḍīs). || 38 ||

There are ten channels (*nāḍī*) which are as follows: *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, *suṣumnā*, *gāndhārī*, *hastijihvā*, *pūṣā*, *alambuṣā*, *kuhū*, and *śaṅkhinī*. Such are the channels. *Iḍā* is the name of the channel on the right; *piṅgalā* is the name of the channel on the left; *suṣumnā* is the name of the channel in the middle. There is also a channel that goes upward to the nose; it is divided into three parts within the nose, with one covering the middle. The reason there are two nostrils is because finally, another channel goes to the crown of the head. The reason it is called the *śivadvāra* (Gate of Śiva) is because it further extends to the crown of the head, and from there it travels to the fingers and toes, spreading and pervading, circulating and settling throughout those limbs. That channel is indeed pervasive; it spreads throughout the entire body and emerges through the skin, forming what is known as the "tree-fiber" (*puhunvulu*). Those are the internal channels; such are all the channels.
These ten principal channels are traditionally known as the carriers of the vital breaths:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.

Ten vital breaths (prāṇas) have been enumerated as defined by Śiva. All these channels (nāḍīs), however many they may be, are pervaded by the wind; there are ten varieties of it. Their forms are: prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, vyāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. Such are the varieties of the wind. Although its forms are very numerous, one must search for them again and again, for their colors are manifold.
Prāṇa is indeed in the mouth, apāna is below, samāna is situated in the heart;
udāna is to be known in the head, and vyāna is in all the joints of the limbs.
(41) This wind is prāṇa; it resides in the nostrils, taking the breath as its object, and it is located at the top of the head. It is that which draws in all the winds.
By what is the downward wind, the *apāna*, established so that it carries away the semen and urine, as well as excrement and phlegm, and causes them to flow out?
// 42 // This *apāna* wind strikes at the lower part of the body; it carries away the semen and urine, and likewise the excrement and phlegm, causing them to flow out. // 42 //

The wind named Samāna, which moves through the limbs with equal course, should expel yellow food, blood, bile, and phlegm. (43) This Samāna wind resides in the heart; its function is to digest what has been eaten, such that it causes the essence of what was eaten to produce feces, the essence of what was drunk to produce urine, and the essence of what was consumed as food to produce sweat, tears, and mucus. Such is the activity of this Samāna wind within the heart.
The wind named udāna agitates the vital points (marmas).
Where does the udāna wind reside? It is sought in the head; it is sought in the eyelids, as well as in the hair of the body, and it causes the growth of the hair.

The *vyāna* wind is described as being distributed throughout; the *vyāna* provokes disease. It moves everywhere and causes agitation; through that wind, there occurs old age. (45) This *vyāna* wind resides in all the joints of the limbs. It searches for, gathers, and distributes [substances]; it performs various types of activities in joining all the joints of the body, as well as causing forgetfulness, agitation, and senility.
Nāga is said to be in the upward belching; Kūrma resides in the opening of the eyes; Kṛkara is indeed in the sneeze, and Devadatta in the yawning. (46)

The wind that is *Nāga* performs the function of moving; the wind that is *Kūrma* performs the function of expansion; the wind that is *Kṛkara* performs the function of carrying away; the wind that is *Devadatta* performs the function of causing yawning; and the wind that is *Dhanañjaya* is the one that performs the function of producing sound. At the time of death, when one does not rise from the bed, that wind which is *Dhanañjaya* remains. All these winds are indeed one, yet because their functions are manifold, their distinctions are many. This is why it is said that there are "many" in the singular unity of the wind. It is this very [wind] that connects the *ātman* with the body, making its perception firm. This is why the noble *ātman* departs to other worlds. Now, as for what is called "other worlds," there are five states (*pañcapada*) which you must know as the destinations to which the *ātman* and the body go.
The gross waking state, composed of diverse things, is perceived directly through the senses;
the dream state is like foam, waves, and bubbles—illusory and flickering;
and the state of deep sleep is a dense darkness of blindness, utterly unmanifest and absolute.
The wise call this subtle, inconceivable, and imperishable state Nirvana. 47

There is the state of waking (*jāgrapada*); there is the state of dreaming (*svapnapada*); there is the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptapada*); there is the state of the fourth (*tūryapada*); and there is the state beyond the fourth (*tūryāntapada*). These five states constitute the stages of the noble Self (*ātman*). This is why they are called the "five stages. As for the state of waking: it occurs during the time of being awake; that waking state is not indistinct. Thus, the noble Self is directly perceived and visible. He who is thus is named *Viśva*. Furthermore, as for the state of dreaming: it is not manifest, like an illusion (*māyā*) existing within the void (*vyoma*). When one awakens from that void, the illusion is seen; when that void ceases, the illusion is no longer seen. Such is the nature of the Self when it is not manifest, because all these states are the manifestations of the Self. He who is thus is named *Taijasa*. When in the state of deep sleep: it is the time of profound slumber. Its nature is emptiness, unconsciousness, and *nirvāṇa*; it is inactive, invisible, and beyond perception. Such is the nature of the state of deep sleep. Thus, the noble Self loses its consciousness and enters into unconsciousness. It is devoid of perception, with forgetfulness as its inherent nature. He who is thus is named *Śrīpada*. These three—the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states—are the supports of the Self. This is what is called the "cycle of the Self" (*ātmasaṃsāra*), where consciousness revolves through the realms of gods, humans, and animals, and experiences heaven and hell. But as for the state of the fourth (*tūryapada*), that is indeed the "Self-perfection" (*ātmasiddhi*). It is understood through the sequence of yoga and the state beyond the fourth (*tūryāntapada*). However, those states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep do not truly dissolve into the Self. Just as their existence is in the waking state, so too is their existence in the dreaming and deep sleep states. Their indicators are: being awake, being asleep, dreaming, and sleeping. Such also are the objects of the entire world. The Lord Vṛhaspati spoke: "The Self exists in the state of waking. When it sleeps, it disappears and is forgotten by the entire world. It is equivalent to death. What is the opposite? It is most fitting to say that the minister has died; he is gone and will not be seen again. For the Self, having disappeared, returns to perceive again. Its indicator is what the son of the Lord says, for whoever perceives is called the conscious Lord (*bhaṭāra cetana*). Therefore, it is not fitting that the conscious part of the Self should sleep, for it wakes up again. What then is the indicator of this? The Lord spoke: "That is why I ask about all these principles. That which is the principle of primordial matter (*pradhānatattva*) is unconscious and has forgetfulness as its inherent nature. The Self pervades the principle of primordial matter, yet it does not forget, because primordial matter causes the forgetfulness of the Self. While abiding in the principle of primordial matter, the Self is in a state of sleeping, which is the opposite [of waking]. The Lord Vṛhaspati spoke: "This is a doubt in the mind of the son of the Lord, concerning the alternating state of the Self and the principle of primordial matter. That forgetfulness is the undifferentiated (*niṣkala*) state of the Self in the perception of the son of the Lord, because consciousness arises from forgetfulness. Consciousness means that which perceives pleasure and pain. Pleasure and pain are the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). Since the cycle of rebirth is perceiving, therefore it is not fitting that perception should be called 'special' (*viśeṣa*). Rather, forgetfulness is what is called 'special,' because it does not perceive pleasure and pain. Thus spoke the Lord Vṛhaspati. The Lord spoke: "Ah, my child! You have been addressed by me, O Vṛhaspati. You said that forgetfulness is 'special. Forgetfulness is unconsciousness. That which is unconscious is desired by the conscious. The analogy is like grass used to make a mat: the one who makes the mat is the one who desires it; the grass itself is unconscious, because it does not perceive. A person is conscious; that which is unconscious is made by him. The mat is woven in various ways according to the will of the conscious one. He desires to produce it. It is just like that, like the one who makes the mat. It is just like that, O Lord: the unconscious is moved by the desire of the conscious. Forgetfulness is the very essence of the unconscious. Therefore, it is not fitting that you call the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) 'special. Thus spoke the Lord. The Lord spoke: "Ah, my child! You have been addressed by me, O Vṛhaspati. Why do you repeatedly speak of these positions? Once the consciousness of the sleeping one has vanished, that is liberation (*mokṣa*). He has departed; let him not perceive again, for that is what you call 'special. Is there any form of 'special' that can be seen? Once it existed, it vanished; once it vanished, it existed. Thus is that which is called 'special. Thus is that which is called the ultimate reality. This is what is called 'perverted knowledge' (*jñāna-viparīta*). It is like a blind man groping in the dark. This is what is called the knowledge of the wise. The Lord Vṛhaspati spoke: "What then is the ultimate reality? This is the command of the Lord. Grant your grace, O son of the Lord. Thus spoke the Lord Vṛhaspati. The Lord spoke: "Thus spoke the Lord. (End of dialogue). (Note: The final repetition "Thus spoke the Lord" appears to be a scribal or editorial closing marker.)

Abandoned by the state of being, devoid of the state of non-being, free from both the states of being and non-being, ending in the partless, and without characteristics. (48) "That which is neither being nor non-being" means that there is no specific distinction; there is no head, and likewise no limbs. Having already been explained as being and non-being, it is therefore neither being nor non-being. It is not fit to be spoken of by the Lord, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it. Likewise, there is no head or limbs. However, here is the means of valid cognition to establish it: [The verse continues: It is not perceived by the senses, yet it is the object of the senses; it is beyond the range of the senses, yet it is the essence of the senses. (49) That which is "not perceived by the senses" means that it cannot be grasped by the five senses such as sight and hearing. Yet, it is "the object of the senses" because it is the support for the functioning of the senses. It is "beyond the range of the senses" because it transcends the domain of the five senses. Yet, it is "the essence of the senses" because it is the very nature of the five senses. [The verse continues: It is not known through inference, yet it is the basis of inference; it is beyond the scope of inference, yet it is the foundation of inference. (50) That which is "not known through inference" means that it cannot be established by logical reasoning. Yet, it is "the basis of inference" because it is the ground upon which inference relies. It is "beyond the scope of inference" because it transcends the reach of logical deduction. Yet, it is "the foundation of inference" because it is the ultimate support for all inferential knowledge. [The verse continues: It is not reached by verbal testimony, yet it is the source of verbal testimony; it is beyond the reach of words, yet it is the root of all speech. (51) That which is "not reached by verbal testimony" means that it cannot be attained through the scriptures or the words of others. Yet, it is "the source of verbal testimony" because it is the origin from which all sacred teachings arise. It is "beyond the reach of words" because it transcends the capacity of language. Yet, it is "the root of all speech" because it is the fundamental cause of every utterance. [The verse continues: It is not perceived by the mind, yet it is the object of the mind; it is beyond the reach of thought, yet it is the essence of the intellect. (52) That which is "not perceived by the mind" means that it cannot be grasped by the internal organ of the mind. Yet, it is "the object of the mind" because it is the focus of mental activity. It is "beyond the reach of thought" because it transcends the sphere of ideation. Yet, it is "the essence of the intellect" because it is the very nature of the cognitive faculty. [The verse continues: It is not known by the self, yet it is the knower of the self; it is beyond the reach of the ego, yet it is the soul of the individual. (53) That which is "not known by the self" means that it cannot be realized by the individual soul (*ātman*). Yet, it is "the knower of the self" because it is that which perceives the self. It is "beyond the reach of the ego" because it transcends the limited sense of "I. Yet, it is "the soul of the individual" because it is the true essence of the person. [The verse continues: It is not seen by the eyes, yet it is the seer of the eyes; it is beyond the range of vision, yet it is the light of the visual faculty. (54) That which is "not seen by the eyes" means that it cannot be beheld by the physical eye. Yet, it is "the seer of the eyes" because it is that which sees through the eyes. It is "beyond the range of vision" because it transcends the field of visual perception. Yet, it is "the light of the visual faculty" because it is the illumination that enables seeing. [The verse continues: It is not heard by the ears, yet it is the hearer of the ears; it is beyond the range of hearing, yet it is the essence of the auditory faculty. (55) That which is "not heard by the ears" means that it cannot be listened to by the physical ear. Yet, it is "the hearer of the ears" because it is that which hears through the ears. It is "beyond the range of hearing" because it transcends the domain of auditory perception. Yet, it is "the essence of the auditory faculty" because it is the core of the power to hear. [The verse continues: It is not smelled by the nose, yet it is the smeller of the nose; it is beyond the range of smell, yet it is the soul of the olfactory faculty. (56) That which is "not smelled by the nose" means that it cannot be perceived by the physical nose. Yet, it is "the smeller of the nose" because it is that which smells through the nose. It is "beyond the range of smell" because it transcends the field of olfactory perception. Yet, it is "the soul of the olfactory faculty" because it is the life-force of the sense of smell. [The verse continues: It is not tasted by the tongue, yet it is the taster of the tongue; it is beyond the range of taste, yet it is the essence of the gustatory faculty. (57) That which is "not tasted by the tongue" means that it cannot be experienced by the physical tongue. Yet, it is "the taster of the tongue" because it is that which tastes through the tongue. It is "beyond the range of taste" because it transcends the field of gustatory perception. Yet, it is "the essence of the gustatory faculty" because it is the core of the power to taste. [The verse continues: It is not felt by the body, yet it is the feeler of the body; it is beyond the range of touch, yet it is the soul of the tactile faculty. (58) That which is "not felt by the body" means that it cannot be grasped by the physical body. Yet, it is "the feeler of the body" because it is that which feels through the body. It is "beyond the range of touch" because it transcends the field of tactile perception. Yet, it is "the soul of the tactile faculty" because it is the life-force of the sense of touch. [The verse continues: It is not known by the intellect, yet it is the knower of the intellect; it is beyond the reach of understanding, yet it is the essence of consciousness. (59) That which is "not known by the intellect" means that it cannot be comprehended by the discriminative faculty. Yet, it is "the knower of the intellect" because it is that which knows through the intellect. It is "beyond the reach of understanding" because it transcends the scope of intellectual discernment. Yet, it is "the essence of consciousness" because it is the fundamental awareness itself. [The verse continues: It is not born of causes, yet it is the cause of all causes; it is beyond the reach of causality, yet it is the root of all existence. (60) That which is "not born of causes" means that it does not arise from any conditions or factors. Yet, it is "the cause of all causes" because it is the source from which all causal chains originate. It is "beyond the reach of causality" because it transcends the realm of dependent origination. Yet, it is "the root of all existence" because it is the foundation of all that exists. [The verse continues: It is not subject to change, yet it is the changer of all; it is beyond transformation, yet it is the agent of all action. (61) That which is "not subject to change" means that it is immutable and eternal. Yet, it is "the changer of all" because it is that which brings about all transformations. It is "beyond transformation" because it remains forever as it is. Yet, it is "the agent of all action" because it is the impeller of all activity. [The verse continues: It is not bound by time, yet it is the time of all times; it is beyond the reach of chronology, yet it is the essence of the ages. (62) That which is "not bound by time" means that it is not limited by past, present, or future. Yet, it is "the time of all times" because it is the temporal dimension within which all moments occur. It is "beyond the reach of chronology" because it transcends the sequence of time. Yet, it is "the essence of the ages" because it is the reality underlying all eras. [The verse continues: It is not perceived by the world, yet it is the world of all worlds; it is beyond the reach of the universe, yet it is the foundation of all realms. (63)
That ghee which is in milk, and that fire which dwells within wood; the water situated in the sky, and the all-pervading wind;
the dust, the darkness, the invisible mind, and the being in man—likewise, that which is neither existent nor non-existent is not perceived in the external world. (49)

"What do you gain by [producing] fire from wood? It is smokeless and invisible, even though it truly exists. What is it that does not consume the wood? He replied, "It does not exist. "Then it has emerged from the wood; what is the benefit of that? "How can you maintain such a thing? "In the same way, there is oil from milk. He replied, "That is merely the appearance of the milk. He said, "There is indeed oil. "How then does it emerge? "External objects are like that, even when they are characterized; they cannot be destroyed. "This is your position, which is called *viśeṣa* (the particular). Smoke is distinct from external objects. Just as with fire and oil, so too is the Lord (*saṅ hyaṅ*) *viśeṣa*; he cannot be characterized and is difficult to destroy. What do you gain from him? He is subtle, without characteristics, and extremely difficult to grasp; that is what is called *viśeṣa*. For if the Lord exists, he can be perceived, and he can be reached within *saṃsāra*. If you maintain that he does not exist, it would be as if the entire world did not exist—this would be a great loss. Therefore, your position is wrong. Furthermore, regarding the disappearance of the *ātman* at its proper time, it enters into the *pradhānatattva*, because the *pradhānatattva* causes that *ātman* to forget itself. Why does that which has entered not die? Because it has forgotten its body. Now, how is it that you say this? That is why the five winds (*pañcavāyu*) were taught previously; they serve as the fuel for the *ātman*. That is what prevents the one who has entered from dying. Bhagavān Vṛhaspati said: "That is what the Lord has spoken. To explain those five winds: when the substance [of the *ātman*] resides in the consciousness of the Lord’s son, it follows along with his own body, using those winds as fuel. What is that fire? Its manifestation exists within the body, so that the consciousness of the Lord’s son may be sustained. The Lord spoke: "He replied: (Note: The final sentence "He replied" indicates the transition to the next section of the dialogue.)
This son of great skill, likewise a knower of the science of reality, is called Bṛhaspati here; he is wise and a seeker of heaven. || 50 ||

“O Vṛhaspati, you have performed a good deed for me by coming to the world of the gods (*svarga*), because you, O wise one among poets, know all the *tattvas* (principles) along with the essence of what has been taught; that is why you were summoned. However, this secret is extremely profound; it was not previously revealed by you in the assembly, as you thought it to be empty. Indeed, this is called ‘the junction of practice’ (*prayogasandhi*), kept secret by the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*). Thus spoke the Lord. Venerable Vṛhaspati replied: “O Son of the Lord, let there be no further doubt. That which the Lord calls ‘consciousness’ (*cetana*) is the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvabhāva*); that is the very thing being perceived. ‘Two’ (*rva*) means knowing and being known. As long as there is knowing, as long as there is being known, so it appears to the Son of the Lord, because it is a particularity (*viśeṣa*). The Lord said: “It is without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). Let it be so, for if it is without characteristics, then the perception of the Son of the Lord is likewise. The Son of the Lord asked: “Please dispel my doubt. Thus spoke Venerable Vṛhaspati: “Do not remain fixed upon consciousness as being without characteristics if it is the consciousness of ultimate reality (*paramārthacetana*). That is the reason for the threefold division of consciousness, as mentioned previously. That is what was stated before, serving as the essence of all principles (*tattva*): the principle of Supreme Śiva (*paramaśivatattva*), the principle of Sadāśiva (*sadāśivatattva*), and the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*). “The principle of Śiva is bliss (*sukha*) that does not revert to suffering. The principle of Sadāśiva is bliss that is neither pure nor impure. The principle of Supreme Śiva is partless (*niṣkala*) and such that its bliss cannot be destroyed. It is difficult to define. But it is as if I am deluded in explaining it, because it is not manifest in the perception of humans; for their nature is limited knowledge (*kiñcidjñāna*). Their understanding is slight, their power is small, their lifespan is short, and they are filled with delusion and afflictions (*kleśa*). Such things are abandoned from their perception; even their knowledge of the principles is lost. Because it is abandoned, certainty regarding the knowledge of the principles is indeed difficult; therefore, it is hidden. Such is the nature of their knowledge. “Such is the nature of what is called a human being, who is surpassed by the gods. You, O Vṛhaspati, are a sage in heaven; do not be arrogant, do not hasten toward knowledge, for it is inconceivable and supremely profound. Even those who are the teachers of poetry [struggle with it]. But as for that principle, it is the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*). That which perceives is consciousness; that which is perceived is the principle of Illusion (*māyātattva*), because the principle of Illusion is wavering, fluctuating, unstable, and never reaching a state of equilibrium—that is what is called ‘Illusion. That which was previously called the ‘particularity’ (*viśeṣa*) is the reason it is called the principle of Illusion. “Now, what is this ‘Illusion’? Illusion is the mind (*manas*) that wavers, because it is joined with the power (*śakti*) of the Person (*puruṣa*). What is this ‘power’? It is the omniscient one, the performer of all actions. When the power of the Person disappears, it pervades Illusion; that is the end of the principle of Illusion. But when the principle of Illusion disappears, its offspring is the principle of Pradhāna (*pradhānatattva*). This is the multitude of the principle of Illusion; its manifestation is that which causes the Person to forget, because one forgets through the principle of Pradhāna. That is why the Self (*ātman*) is called ‘Person’ (*puruṣa*): ‘he lies much’ (*puru śete*). ‘Much’ (*puru*) refers to the state of being great (*kaḍatvan*); the Self is the greatness of the principle of Pradhāna. In that he lies, the Self is manifested; that is why the Self is called ‘Person. That is what is called ‘perceiving’; it is termed ‘the transmigrating consciousness’ (*cetanasaṃsāra*). That is what is called the ‘particularity,’ which is beyond the principle of Illusion. “That which is the principle of Pradhāna is something else entirely; that is why it is without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), because it cannot be destroyed. Therefore, you must strive; do not be arrogant. He is the essence of what is sought; he is not far from your knowledge. That is the object of your meditation. Thus spoke the Lord. Venerable Vṛhaspati replied: [End of dialogue].
What is the knowledge that accomplishes the path, and what is the supreme vow of austerity? O Śiva, having honored me, please explain this to me according to the truth.

"O Lord, please explain the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*) and its reasoning, by means of which one may attain that which is called the Holy One (*saṅ hyaṅ viśeṣa*), the cause of attainment. What are the forms of austerity (*tapa*) and observance (*brata*)? How does one show love for the Son of the Lord? And how does one traverse the various paths of austerity and observance? Thus spoke Bhagavān Vṛhaspati. The Lord replied, saying: "My teaching is exceedingly divine. Herein is the means of attaining that which is called the Holy One, the supreme goal (*parāmartha*)."
Liberation is attained through three causes: from the preeminence of knowledge, from the path of non-attachment to the senses, and from the destruction of the defects of craving. (52)

There are three kinds of *sādhana* (means of realization) by which one who desires liberation may practice: *jñānābhyudreka*, which is the knowledge of all principles (*tattva*); *indriyāyogamārga*, which is not being restless toward sense objects; and *tṛṣṇādoṣākṣaya*, which is the extinguishing of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious karma. These are the three. Thus they are practiced. This is the means of practicing them; its essence is indeed the *gōnta* (the central point). It is like a net that covers its center: when it is struck, all its meshes are affected. In the same way, knowledge remains hidden within the *gōnta*. If you say, "What is this?"—consciousness (*cetanā*) is the intense light within knowledge. "Light" (*prakāśa*) means that which does not require fuel, does not depend on darkness, and is not measured by the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). It is eternally manifest and free from obstruction, for it is the Lord (*Bhaṭāra*). He is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) within the body. Therefore, one should practice meditation (*abhyāsa*) more and more, for that is its nature when practiced. Once consciousness has been practiced, the fruit of the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is certain. The venerable Vṛhaspati spoke: "O Son of the Lord, there is another position (*pakṣa*) to be heard. Life is the cause of the assembly of this body. That is what produces it; its manifestation is as follows: when a person falls ill, even if they are well-fed or even poisoned, their life-span ends. There is a distinction between the body and the illness of that body; that is what is called death. Death means disappearance, beyond support. Such is the manifestation of the body; it is good to produce such a life.
