In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), that which lives is indeed *saṃsāra*, and that which dies is called *mokṣa*, because it disappears completely and no longer experiences suffering. Such was the statement of the other position. The Lord commanded: "The Lord spoke: 'Do not discuss this in the assembly (*sabhā*). That position is merely a fabrication. How many eyes have been lost? If that which is seen is shown, what is death, which is the absence of further birth? What of the auspicious and inauspicious karma performed? Your statement lacks proof. Here is the divine Sun (*Āditya*), who is directly perceived. You know him through his source and his appearance; you know his source and his appearance. If you say, "He is the essence of the one who has arisen," or "He is the one who has arisen now"—if you say that, he is behind you and hidden. If he were visible, you would know him directly. Or if you say, "Many have arisen," or "Many have arisen now"—if you say that, what is his form? He is not clearly manifest. Where do you see the collection of the divine Sun? Where do you know his quantity? That is why he is requested to be "many. But if he were manifest, you would know all of that. Therefore, those instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are not appropriate: seeing and looking. That is the position of humans; it is extremely contrary. It is delusion and darkness, lacking the lamp. Even during the day, it causes confusion regarding the very tip of the nose. That is the reason for using the instruments of knowledge when applied to the divine Lord, for they are the basis for speech. Because knowledge is not established therein, that is why, O Vṛhaspati, you must strive; do not be negligent. Regarding words that seek to establish proof: the divine Lord is the pinnacle of speech and the nature of the instruments of knowledge. As for the time of death, the self (*ātman*) in the body remains for a thousand years along with the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*). Only the physical parts disappear; the self remains without perishing, for it is the supporter of the entire world. Therefore, the self is manifested. The five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*) serve as its body, along with the ten senses, intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. After passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and the latent impressions of karma (*karmavāsanā*) have all dissolved, the self is formed. That which makes the five subtle elements into a body is the body of the self at the time of death. Why is there rebirth? Because the consciousness (*citta*) has already merged with the body. Its manifestation is such that there is no person who is not attached to sense objects. A living person desires food, sleep, fear, and sexual union; they are afraid of death and suffering; they desire to eat and drink, they hate what is unpleasant. Such is the nature of birth. That consciousness in the body is thus; it bears no fruit in its perception, for it deposits all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) into the self. In the ultimate state, there is no further birth. However, the ascetic (*viku*) who is able to transcend sense objects and the lord of yoga (*yogīśvara*) attains complete liberation (*kamokṣan*). For the five subtle elements that form the body of the self are minute; therefore it is called the *sūkṣmaśarīra* (subtle body). That is the body of the self. When it becomes a body in the hell-world (*narakaloka*), it carries [the self] there, making *saṃsāra* its experience. If its past actions in the human state were heavy, that is the cause for going to hell. If its past actions in the human state were good, that is the reason for having a body in heaven (*svarga*), making happiness its experience. If its past actions in the human state were neither heavy nor good, that is the reason for being born again as a human. Having escaped from the weight or goodness of past actions in the human state, how is its future state obtained? One who is able to practice the Lord’s vows (*brata*) is good. If one does not know the state of a *yogīśvara* during one's life, one will perish and be born again. But if one attains the state of a *yogīśvara*, that is a distinction in one's future state. There are three types of future states: *karman*, *jñāna*, and *yogin*. *Karman* refers to one whose vows are physical: performing worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and being diligent. Whatever effort they exert in their practice, the fruit of that exertion is offered to the Lord and to guests. That is what is called *karman*. *Jñāna* refers to... (text breaks off).

He knows all the deities within himself, as well as the principles of the worlds (*bhuvanatattva*). He possesses knowledge that is clear and profound; indeed, it is the hall of the Lord residing within his body. Therefore, he is truly tranquil: he does not worship, he does not offer oblations, he does not perform rituals, nor does he engage in various activities. He finds contentment in knowledge; he is not driven by worldly impulses. He constantly cultivates only pure consciousness (*cetana*), for it is pleasant to know the distinction from the Self (*nirātman*); it cannot be destroyed, nor can it be led astray. This is why there are three means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*): namely, from the teacher (*guru*), from the scriptures (*śāstra*), and from oneself (*svataḥ*). "From the teacher" means the oral instructions of the Guru. "From the scriptures" means the teachings accompanied by the methods of practice found in the scriptures. "From oneself" means that within one's own body, one attains that Supreme Being (*saṅ hyaṅ viśeṣa*). This is the method of the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*); it is called the "hub of the net. That which was previously taught to you is this very thing. Now, as for what is called Yoga: there are six types of yoga, which are known as *ṣaḍaṅgayoga*.
Withdrawal of the senses, as well as meditation, breath control,
concentration, deliberation, and absorption— this is called the six-limbed yoga.

Now, as for that which is called the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*): it is the means for one who desires to attain the supreme and particular state of the Lord. One must exert oneself; do not be distracted by the teachings of the sages. There is what is called *pratyāhārayoga*, there is what is called *dhyānayoga*, there is what is called *prāṇāyāmayoga*, there is what is called *dhāraṇayoga*, there is what is called *tarkayoga*, and there is what is called *samādhiyoga*. Such is the six-limbed yoga. Now, as for this *pratyāhārayoga*:

Withdrawing the senses from their objects—the sense-fields—with effort and with a tranquil mind, is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). [This means] withdrawing all the senses from their respective objects; the *citta*, *buddhi*, and *manas* do not follow one after another; the *citta* is restrained and made to remain still. This is what is known as *pratyāhārayoga*.

That form which is meditated upon constantly—free from dualities, free from modification, tranquil, and likewise immovable—is called *dhyāna*. That is knowledge; it is without transformation; it is ever-present and constant; it is always without obstruction; that alone is what is known as *dhyānayoga*.
When all the gates [of the body] are closed and the wind is restrained within, and the head is pierced by the wind, that is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*. (56)

All the gates—the eyes, nose, mouth, and ears—are closed. The wind that was previously exhaled now returns; it is drawn back and made to circulate within the crown of the head. However, if one has not practiced the wind, it will not circulate there; instead, it will circulate within the nose. Nevertheless, it must be done with great care when drawing the wind [back]. This is what is called *prāṇāyāmayoga*.

Having established the syllable *oṃ* in the heart, which is of the nature of Śiva when dissolved into reality (*tattva*), it is called *dhāraṇā* (concentration) because the syllable *oṃ* is held there. The word *hana* means "to strike" (*umuṅgv iṅ hati*). Because one strikes through concentration (*yateka dhāraṇān*), and because one does not waver (*yapvan hilaṅ ika*) during the time of yoga, that is what is meant by "having the nature of Śiva" (*śivātmā*). When Lord Śiva is thus [absorbed], that is what is called *dhāraṇā-yoga*.

One should constantly contemplate that form as being like space—space that is eternal, firm, and soundless; that is called *tarka*. (58) Space is indeed the reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, it is like space, for there is no sound within it. That which corresponds to the ultimate truth is such that it is not merely wavering or fluctuating; this alone is what is called *tarkayoga*.
One should constantly contemplate that which is indifferent, free from conceptualization, desireless, peaceful, immutable, and signless; by this, it is called samādhi. 59

That knowledge which is beyond indifference, beyond conceptualization, beyond the existence of desire within it, and beyond the existence of mental cultivation within it—wherein even the subtlest veil has not yet been removed, nor can it be removed; wherein that consciousness is not yet a manifest entity, because it still perceives this body and remains outside the fourfold conceptualization. What is called the "fourfold conceptualization" (caturkalpanā)? It consists of: knowing and being known; the one who knows and the act of knowing. These are what is meant by the fourfold conceptualization. All of these are absent in the Lord of Yogins (yogīśvara); therefore, this is called Samādhi-yoga. This is what is called the Six-Limbed Yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), which serves as the knowledge of the wise and is the means by which the Supreme Being (saṅ hyaṅ viśeṣa) is attained. Such is the state of the Lord of Yogins; thus he is protected in the tenfold ethical conduct (daśaśīla).
Non-violence, celibacy, truthfulness that is not worldly, and non-stealing—
these five are the restraints (yamas) proclaimed by Rudra.
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, and moderation in food [are the observances].
And heedfulness—these five are proclaimed as the observances. || 61 ||

Non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) means not to cause harm. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) means not to engage in sexual intercourse. Truthfulness (*satya*) means not speaking falsely. Non-contentiousness (*avyavahārika*) means being without dispute, without litigation, and without finding fault in others. Non-stealing (*astainya*) means not coveting, not seizing the property of another that does not belong to both parties. Freedom from anger (*akrodha*) means not being prone to frequent outbursts of rage. Service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) means devotion toward the teacher. Purity (*śauca*) means daily recitation of prayers and purification of the body. Moderation in food (*āhāralāghava*) means not eating excessively. Heedfulness (*apramāda*) means not being negligent; it is the constant mindfulness of life as the means for practicing *yoga-samādhi*. One must not be indolent; one must apply oneself to these means. "Means" (*sādhana*) refers to the path of *yoga*, which has the ten virtues (*daśaśīla*) as its basis. These ten virtues produce *yoga*. This consists of that which is maintained and that which is practiced. Thus, the one who exerts effort to cultivate these two—virtue (*śīla*) and knowledge (*jñāna*)—is what is meant by "heedfulness. Such are the ten virtues; they protect the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*) in his *samādhi*. Now, when the Lord of Yogins seeks such knowledge, that is called the "Fourth State" (*tūryapada*). When that knowledge is attained, it transcends the body and transcends the principle of illusion (*māyātattva*); that is the "State Beyond the Fourth" (*tūryāntapada*). For he is one who is "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*), meaning liberation follows even while alive. This is because he attains the partless state (*niṣkala*) during the time of *samādhi*, yet his body does not perish. This is because the latent impressions of karma (*karmavāsanā*) continue until they are exhausted, having been burned away by the fire of *yoga*. This is how one destroys impurity (*mala*): the waking state (*jagrapada*) meets with the Fourth State (*tūryapada*). Upon their meeting, there are the seven limbs, the seven fires, and the seven nectars. As for the "seven limbs": [the following list follows].
Earth, water, fire, air, space, intellect, and mind—listen, this is called the sevenfold limb (saptāṅga).
Earth, water, fire, air, space, intellect, and mind: these are what is meant by the "seven limbs. Now, as for the "seven fires":
The smeller, the taster, the seer, the toucher, and the hearer; as well as the thinker and the knower—listen, these are called the seven fires. (63)

The "smeller" (ghrātā) is one who smells; the "taster" (rasayitā) is one who tastes the six flavors; the "seer" (draṣṭā) is one who sees; the "toucher" (spraṣṭā) is one who touches; the "hearer" (śrotā) is one who hears; the "thinker" (mantā) is one who conceptualizes; the "knower" (boddhā) is one who understands. These are what is meant by the "seven fires. This is the nature of the principles (tattva) to be understood by the Lord of Yogins (yogīśvara). The reason for this is that the impurities (mala) residing within his body have been purified. Now, as for the "seven nectars" (saptāmṛta):
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are declared; volition and the object of cognition—these seven are called nectar. (64)

Sound is heard; touch is felt; form is seen; taste is tasted; smell is smelled; conceptualization and non-conceptualization; that which is to be known is understood. These seven are called the "Immortals" (*amṛta*). All these are what is to be known by the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*), as well as the latent impressions of karma (*karmavāsanā*). Regarding their definition: he restrains every object whatsoever that is conceptualized by him. "Restraint" (*saṃyama*) means the performance of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*. That is what is called restraint. It is easy for him to understand all of these; therefore, he is always absorbed in the Lord. Furthermore, because he is absorbed in the Lord, he is forever free from suffering; therefore, the Lord is his protector.
This divine Agni burns away a well-accumulated heap of evil;
thereafter, he fulfills one's thoughts, just as Śiva is a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi). 65

The weight of his sins, O Lord of Yogins, along with all residual impressions (*vāsanā*), are cast into the Śiva-fire by the Lord; at the end, those karmic impressions vanish. He no longer needs to exert himself in *samādhi*, nor does the Lord need to depend upon him who is thus [perfected]. This is why he is a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*): whatever he desires comes to pass, and whatever he wishes becomes so; yet, as for its manifestation, he attains that mastery over the elements (*kāṣṭaiśvaryan*).
Aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, and prāpti;

as well as prākāmya, īśitva, vaśitva, and yatrakāmatva. [66] What is aṇimā? What is laghimā? What is mahimā? What is prāpti? What is prākāmya? What is īśitva? What is vaśitva? What is yatrakāmāvasāyitva? Now, this is what aṇimā is:
Just as the body, having become extremely subtle, leaves behind its gross form at will, it becomes minute and traverses the three worlds; therefore, this power is called *aṇimā*.

Water descends into the earth; that which causes it to flow downward is called *alita*. It means being able to know that which is unknown, entering and emerging like a bee moving through a lotus stalk. In this way, the Lord of Yogis enters and emerges from the earth; there is no obstruction in his movement. Even if he encounters mountains or rocks, he passes through them continuously, and they do not block him. Thus his body disappears; this is what is called *aṇimā*. Now, as for *laghimā*: having previously possessed heaviness, one suddenly abandons it.

One’s body shall become as light as cotton; likewise, there is *laghimā* (levity) according to one’s will. (68) Just as a piece of cotton can float upward, so too the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*) possesses this power of will. Whatever he desires to give—whether it be heaven, the seven continents (*saptadvīpa*), or the seven underworlds (*saptapātāla*)—he can bestow them. He can even cause the entire cosmic egg (*aṇḍabhuvana*) to tremble. Mastery over all things is his; this is what is called *laghimā*. Now, as for *mahimā* (greatness): [text continues]

Wherever one may go by one's own will, there one dwells according to that will; because one is honored everywhere, it is called "greatness" (mahimā). [This means: One goes to another region with ease, yet one is honored here with all enjoyments, such as food and so forth, starting from oneself; this is what is meant by greatness. Now, this is attainment (prāpti): yatraiva svecchayā gacchet tatra tatsvecchavāsitam | sarvataḥ pūjyate yasmān mahimā tena procyate || 69 [The commentary explains: Wherever one may go by one's own will, there one dwells according to that will; because one is honored everywhere, it is called "greatness. [This means: One goes to another region with ease, yet one is honored here with all enjoyments, such as food and so forth, starting from oneself; this is what is meant by greatness. Now, this is attainment (prāpti):
Therefore, it should be understood as residing within the substrate, like a latent desire;
for the attainment of all things whatsoever, that which is called "attainment" (prāpti) exists everywhere here.

This is the power of mastery (*asiṅ sakahyun*) of the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*). Regarding all things (*sarvavastu*), they come to him spontaneously; he neither seeks them nor asks for them. Whatever those various things may be—whether they are the accumulated latent impressions of karma (*karmavāsanā*) that yield the fruit of happiness for him, or when he experiences that happiness because of his fear of the exhaustion of the fruits of karma—he thereby creates thousands of bodies. Even though he possesses a hundred bodies, he is capable of attaining heaven. Once he has finished experiencing all those enjoyments (*bhukti*)—whether they be excellent offspring, or objects of enjoyment (*bhoga*), secondary enjoyment (*upabhoga*), and total enjoyment (*paribhoga*)—he becomes liberated (*viśāta*). He is no longer obstructed by the fruits of his good deeds; this is what is called attainment (*prāpti*). Now, as for what is called the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*):

The form created by oneself would indeed be attained by means of the self; whatever form is created according to one's desire is declared to be *prākāmya*. Whatever is desired—whether it be the state of a lord of yogins (*yogīśvara*), a god, a human, or an animal—whatever he gives or whatever he makes his own, that is what is called *prākāmya*. Now, as for *īśitva*: *Yathecchā saṅ yogīśvara / asiṅ sakahyun ira rūpa nira / yan hyaṅ / yan mānuṣa / yan tiryak / kapva ikān dadi nira / pinakatĕmahanira / yeka prākāmya ṅaranya //* "Whatever is desired by the lord of yogins—whatever form he manifests, whether divine, human, or animal—whatever he gives or makes his own, that is what is called *prākāmya*. Now, as for *īśitva*:

If one always goes to the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Sūrya for the sake of devotion favorable to the gods, this is called *īśitva*. Just as it is said in the scriptures that one is able to ascend to the worlds of the venerable Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Sūrya, one is indeed able to visit all those deities, because our Lord exists within the *yogīśvara*; that is the reason why one is able to reach all those deities. This is what is meant by *īśitva*. Now, as for *vaśitva*:

Wherever there is mastery (*vaśitva*), through that mastery there is the state of acting according to one's will (*yatrakāmatā*). (73) Vena Siromutu is the lord of all the deities; he dwells within their very hearts, for he is the sovereign substance (*makadravya*) of the entire kingdom. If they do not obey him, that is what is called "mastery" (*vaśitva*). Now, as for this "ability to resolve according to one's will" (*yatrakāmāvasāyitva*): The ability to resolve according to one's will is the state where the desire to go to a particular place is fulfilled by the body itself. (74b)

Irika ta sirān maṅka tāvak nira / dumaṇḍa ikaṅ deva mānuṣa tiryak / asiṅ laṅghana ri sira / yeka yatrakāmāvasāyitva ṅaranya // (In this regard, his power extends over gods, humans, and animals; whatever he desires to transcend, he does so; that is what is called *yatrakāmāvasāyitva*. Such are the eight sovereign powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), which are all the fruits of the Lord of Yogins. When the concentration (*samādhi*) of the Lord of Yogins is sharp, he shakes the principles (*tattva*) below the *pradhānatattva*. He focuses upon the principle of the three qualities (*triguṇatattva*). When he is struck by his own concentration, he encounters the disturbances (*upasarga*) of the three qualities. This is what causes the Lord of Yogins to enter a state of possession (*umāveśa*); all of them act as obstacles (*vighna*). Their forms are as follows: there is that called *darśana* (vision), there is that called *śravaṇa* (hearing), there is that called *boddhavya* (the knowable), and there is that called *gandha* (smell). *Darśana* means that at the time of yoga, one sees forms like those of deities. *Śravaṇa* means that a subtle sound resounds, as if bestowing the essence of spiritual perfection (*siddhi*) at the time of yoga. Furthermore, much knowledge is encountered by him at the time of yoga; wisdom increases, and he understands the meaning of the teachings when he studies them. *Boddhavya* means that it is as if the scent of royalty enters the nostrils at the time of yoga. That is what is called *gandha*. All these are the disturbances of *sattva*. Now, the disturbances of *rajas*: there is that which causes him to feel distressed; his mind becomes agitated at the time of yoga. There is that which causes him to feel as if struck; there is that which causes him to feel as if being pushed and prodded while his mind is agitated. There is that which causes him to feel as if being pulled and jerked. There is that which causes his mind to feel as if it were buzzing. There is that which causes his mind to feel as if it were stuck in mud. All these are the disturbances of *rajas*. Now, the disturbances of *tamas*: there is that which causes him to feel as if he is sinking at the time of yoga. There is that which causes him to feel as if he is fainting; there is a sense of nausea in his mind. There is that which causes his limbs to feel as if they are being stuffed with cotton while his mind is agitated. There is that which causes his mind to become dark. There is that which causes the mind to be inverted, such that he forgets the nature of his consciousness. All these are the disturbances of *tamas*. When these disturbances are encountered by him at the time of yoga, he must exert effort. He should perform external counter-measures: making sounds of "mā-puyapuya," "malĕṅalĕṅa," clapping his hands repeatedly, and rubbing his ears. This is because it is said, "The counter-measure is the remedy. That is why he must remain vigilant regarding his knowledge of external medicinal herbs. When he has finished his practice, he should return to performing yoga. The concentration (*samādhi*) escapes from that body; do not let the body be agitated. Do not let the knowledge be agitated by focusing on the body, for that is what is called *saṃsāra*. Such is the conduct of my son, O Vṛhaspati. // o //
Thus ends the Vṛhaspatitattva.
